content: 1. Antivenoms must be made accessible to all individuals who require them. Enhancing procurement and distribution systems will help reduce stock shortages in rural areas, while improved surveillance will enable quicker identification of issues related to product quality and safety. 2. National systems for drug procurement, distribution, and surveillance will be strengthened to ensure better access and monitoring. 3. Snakebite envenoming is underreported in most countries, both at sub-national and national levels. Improved data collection and analysis are critical for understanding the burden of the disease and allocating resources effectively. 4. A standardized set of tools and applications, along with clearly defined minimum data requirements, should be established to assess the impact of snakebite envenoming on health systems and communities. 5. Support will be provided to enhance the capacity of health systems to collect, compile, and analyze data on snakebite envenoming. The success of these measures will be determined by the number of countries adopting new or repurposed data collection tools and contributing data to the WHO Global Health Observatory. 6. Snakebite envenoming should be included in national and sub-national health plans to align with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) 2030. This integration ensures recognition of snakebite envenoming as a neglected tropical disease (NTD) and highlights its importance in improving the lives of the world’s poorest populations. 7. In some regions, specific types of snakebite envenoming require additional resources, such as specialized care for long-term renal injury caused by certain snake species. Substantial investments in medical care and consumables are necessary in these cases. 8. National and sub-national programs tailored to specific needs should be supported with appropriate tools, resources, and strategies to address the burden of snakebite envenoming. 9. Enhanced monitoring and surveillance of snakebite envenoming are essential to gather accurate data on disease burden, which will inform economic, health, and social impact modeling. This will ensure appropriate resource allocation to the most affected regions and accelerate the implementation of control strategies. 10. Accurate estimates of the burden of snakebite envenoming at sub-national, national, regional, and global levels will help identify priority areas and resource requirements. 11. Snakebite envenoming is significantly underreported, partly because many cases are not registered in health systems. The most accurate data come from combining information from health systems and communities using various tools and applications. 12. Standardized, comparable, and reliable data collection requires investment in methods, tools, and applications. Robust, standardized software packages and surveillance systems will improve data collection, storage, analysis, and reporting. 13. Measuring the burden of snakebite envenoming requires a standardized minimum set of definitions, harmonized epidemiological parameters, and agreed surveillance methods. Data should be contributed to a common global repository to ensure comparability at all levels. 14. Internationally agreed standards for surveillance, guidance, and harmonization of strategies for snakebite envenoming will be established. A minimum data set and standardized epidemiological parameters will be agreed upon, with data integrated into the WHO Global Health Observatory. 15. Research on the ecology, epidemiology, clinical outcomes, and therapeutics of snakebite envenoming is essential. Poor data quality in most affected countries hinders effective program implementation and evaluation. 16. Baseline data at sub-national and national levels will be published to establish benchmarks for evaluating programs. Consolidated baseline data will be integrated into the Global Health Observatory to establish regional benchmarks. 17. Improving data quality in regions with weak surveillance will fill knowledge gaps about the burden of snakebite envenoming and ensure accurate regional assessments. 18. There is a significant disparity between data from communities and health systems, as many snakebite victims do not seek healthcare. Integrating data from both sources will provide a more accurate assessment of the overall burden. 19. The current gold standard for testing antivenom efficacy involves in vivo testing in laboratory animals. New testing procedures that reduce or eliminate the use of live animals will align with international commitments to ethical research principles and may be more cost-effective. 20. The strategy will encourage research into preclinical models of antivenom safety and efficacy. New preclinical tests adhering to updated animal testing principles will improve data quality and reduce quality control costs. 21. Most antivenoms in use today have not undergone formal clinical trials, and evidence for their safety and effectiveness is often weak. Investment in pragmatic, cost-effective clinical studies will improve understanding of the disease and the efficacy of specific antivenom products. 22. Incorporating cost data into clinical studies will enable better resource allocation by health ministries. The strategy emphasizes support for preclinical and clinical research, including trials, to improve understanding of snakebite envenoming and the affordability of treatments. 23. Field centers for clinical research on snakebite envenoming and sentinel clinical trial sites may be established. Data from well-designed clinical studies will inform policy, procurement, clinical care, and resource allocation decisions. 24. Populations frequently exposed to venomous snakes, such as agricultural workers, are at higher risk of snakebite envenoming. Understanding the ecology and epidemiology of these interactions can guide interventions to reduce or eliminate risks. 25. Additional resources will be directed to areas with high snakebite incidence due to occupational, environmental, or behavioral factors. Epidemiological research will identify high-risk populations and inform prevention strategies. 26. The incidence of snakebite envenoming is rarely uniform across a country or region. Distribution varies based on ecological, geographic, and environmental factors. Research using geospatial tools can provide a clearer picture of incidence and guide resource allocation. 27. Operational research will address challenges in rebuilding a sustainable antivenom market, particularly in regions like sub-Saharan Africa. This will involve analyzing supply and demand, socioeconomic factors, and barriers to efficiency. 28. Tools for assessing the cost-effectiveness of antivenoms will be developed, and economic analyses will recommend ways to improve production, reduce costs, and enhance product quality. 29. Strong partnerships among WHO, member states, development partners, donors, and stakeholders are essential for implementing the strategy. Advocacy, supported by robust data and effective coordination, will build a sound investment case for the strategy. 30. Snakebite envenoming should be integrated into public health programs and national health plans to ensure universal health coverage. Policies should promote equitable access to essential health services for affected populations. 31. Countries should incorporate snakebite envenoming into their SDG and UHC 2030 agendas, identifying necessary actions and publishing progress reports. Regional cooperation in antivenom regulation will strengthen systems and improve access to quality-assured products. 32. Advocacy and effective communication are crucial for building coalitions of partners and stakeholders to operationalize the strategy and secure necessary resources.
